opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, it wasn't one dramatic moment. It was more a gradual realization about where I wanted my work to matter.

I came up through computation. I loved the elegance of algorithms and the satisfaction of making something run faster or more cleanly. But at some point I started asking, "Faster for what? Cleaner for whom?" A lot of the problems I was working on were interesting in the abstract, but I didn't always feel connected to the people on the other end of them.

Health changed that for me. When you start working with clinical data, imaging data, patient outcomes, the stakes become very concrete. Behind every row in a dataset is a person who was sick, scared, hoping for a good answer. That reframes everything. Suddenly the technical choices you make, how you handle missing data, how you validate a model, whether it generalizes to a different hospital or population, aren't just methodological details. They affect whether someone gets the right treatment.

I also found health data intellectually richer than I expected. It's messy, heterogeneous, collected for reasons that have nothing to do with research, full of bias and gaps. For someone with a computational background that's a real challenge. You can't just throw a model at it. You have to understand the clinical context, talk to physicians, understand how the data was generated. That kind of collaboration became one of my favorite parts of the work.

So I'd say the shift wasn't really away from computation. It was toward using computation in service of something I cared about deeply. The tools are the same. The purpose got a lot clearer.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I don't think of it as leaving computation so much as finding the problem that made computation feel urgent. My training was in computer science, and for a long time the work was about the methods themselves: can I get this algorithm to be faster, more elegant, more general. That's satisfying, but at some point I started to feel like I was building very good hammers without ever asking what was worth hitting.

The turn came when I spent time around clinicians, originally in medical imaging. I'd sit in on tumor board or watch a radiologist read a scan, and I'd realize how much judgment was being made on top of enormous amounts of data that nobody had the tools or the time to actually use. A surgeon would be looking at a liver CT and estimating, more or less by eye, how much healthy tissue would be left after a resection. And I'd think, that's a measurement problem. That's something we can quantify, and quantifying it might change what happens to this patient.

So the shift was really about stakes. In pure computation, if my model was wrong, I'd get a worse number on a benchmark. In health, if the model is wrong, someone gets the wrong treatment, or doesn't get treatment they needed. That's frightening, but it's also clarifying. It forces you to care about things computer scientists often wave away: where the data came from, who's missing from it, what the clinician will actually do with the output, whether a prediction is useful at all if it comes without an explanation.

And I'd add that health data is just a genuinely hard and interesting computational problem. It's messy, multimodal, longitudinal, full of missingness that isn't random. The things that make it frustrating are the same things that make it a great place to do real methodological work. So I didn't give up computation. I just found a domain where the computation finally had to answer to something.

That connection between a technical question and its potential impact is what drew me toward health and data analysis.
